cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: The main sources of law in England and Wales are statute law, common law, delegated legislation and international treaties

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: Statute law is made by Parliament — Acts of Parliament are the highest form of domestic law

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: Common law is developed through judicial decisions — judges interpret statutes and create law in new areas

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: Delegated legislation is law made by bodies authorised by Parliament (e.g. statutory instruments, by-laws)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: Parliamentary sovereignty means Acts of Parliament override all other domestic sources of law

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) into UK law

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: EU law had supremacy over UK law while the UK was a member — after Brexit, retained EU law continues to apply unless changed

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: The doctrine of precedent (stare decisis) ensures that lower courts follow decisions of higher courts

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: Law reporting ensures that legal decisions are recorded and accessible for future cases

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: Statutes are interpreted by judges using rules: the literal rule, golden rule and mischief rule

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: Parliament can make or unmake any law — no Parliament can bind a future Parliament

cards.front: Recall a key point about Sources of Law
cards.back: The legislative process involves both Houses of Parliament and Royal Assent before an Act becomes law

cards.front: What should you know about gcse law exam tips — sources of law?
cards.back: 1. For Sources of Law questions, identify the relevant area of law and state the legal principles clearly 2. Apply legal rules to the facts of the scenario — don't just state the law 3. When evaluating, consider both the effectiveness and fairness of legal rules 4. Reference relevant cases and statutes when discussing Sources of Law 5. Consider reform proposals and alternative approaches where relevant
How far does parliamentary sovereignty limit the effectiveness of other sources of law? (15 marks)

AO1 (Knowledge & Understanding): Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of sources of law, including key legal rules, principles and concepts relevant to OCR J271. AO2 (Application): Apply knowledge and understanding of sources of law to legal scenarios and problems, using legal reasoning and analysis. AO3 (Analysis & Evaluation): Analyse, evaluate and critique legal rules, principles and reform
